subject: business
title: Disruptive Innovation: why capable incumbents rationally ignore the threat until it is too late
dek: Clayton M. Christensen and Joseph L. Bower's 1995 Harvard Business Review essay 'Disruptive Technologies: Catching the Wave,' The Innovator's Dilemma (1997), and the clarifying 2015 HBR piece with Michael E. Raynor and Rory McDonald. The framework distinguishes sustaining from disruptive innovation — low-end and new-market footholds, resource-allocation processes that favor best customers, and why the process unfolds over years. Steel mini-mills moving from rebar upward are the teaching case; the 2015 article insists Uber is usually not disruption. Cite only what named public pages state.

glossary.explain: Clayton Christensen's theory: innovation that starts in a low-end or new-market foothold and moves upmarket, eventually displacing established competitors.
Innovation that improves products along the dimensions established customers already value. Incumbents are good at this.
Harvard Business School professor (d. 2020). Author of The Innovator's Dilemma and the theory of disruptive innovation.

sections.title: When doing everything right causes you to lose

blocks.text: In the decades before Clayton Christensen and Joseph Bower published 'Disruptive Technologies: Catching the Wave' in the January–February 1995 Harvard Business Review, the standard managerial advice was clear: listen to your best customers, invest in the technologies they value, improve your products along the dimensions that matter most to the market. Firms that did all of that were admired. The paradox Christensen documented was that capable, well-managed companies could follow that advice faithfully — and still be displaced by competitors they had every reason to ignore until it was too late.

blocks.caption: Clayton M. Christensen, Harvard Business School professor and author of The Innovator's Dilemma. Christensen spent decades refining the theory of disruptive innovation and, in his later work, clarifying what the term does and does not mean.

blocks.text: The core distinction is between sustaining innovation and disruptive innovation. Sustaining innovations make products better along the dimensions established customers already value. Disruptive innovations start by underperforming on traditional metrics but offer lower cost, more convenience, or access for nonconsumers. The 2015 essay distinguishes low-end disruption (serving overserved customers with 'good enough' quality) from new-market disruption (creating markets among people who previously could not afford the product). The process unfolds over years as the disruptor improves and moves upmarket.

Steel mini-mills are Christensen's canonical case. In the 1960s and 1970s, mini-mills using electric arc furnaces entered at the bottom with rebar, which integrated mills did not defend. Mini-mill technology improved, and producers moved upmarket into structural beams and then higher grades. Nucor is the firm most associated with this path.

blocks.caption: Steel mini-mill facility. The canonical disruption case: mini-mills entered at rebar and moved upmarket over decades.

blocks.text: Honda's entry into the U.S. motorcycle market with small, inexpensive bikes (the Supercub) is Christensen's example of new-market disruption. These bikes enabled nonconsumers who would not have bought large touring bikes. Netflix disrupting Blockbuster via DVD-by-mail is another teaching case, though the 2015 essay notes Netflix's streaming did not cleanly fit the original low-end path.

The December 2015 essay exists because 'disruptive innovation' became so popular it lost its meaning. The 2015 piece insists: disruption starts in an unattractive foothold and moves upmarket over years. Uber, despite being widely called disruptive, attacked the mainstream taxi market directly with a superior service — that is competition, not disruption. Misusing the term hides what makes true disruption hard for incumbents to counter.

sections.title: What low-end market are you ignoring?

blocks.text: Look at your organization or an industry you know. Is there a segment at the bottom — overserved customers who would accept 'good enough' for less, or nonconsumers who cannot afford the current offer — that you or the incumbents are rationally ignoring? What would it take to serve that segment?
